text:
JUDGMENT OF THE COURT (Fifth Chamber)

16 July 2026 ( *1 )

[Text rectified by order of 20 July 2026]

(Appeal – EU Financial Regulations – Implementation of the EU budget under joint or indirect management with an international organisation – Decision refusing to recognise an entity as an international organisation with retroactive effect – Concept of ‘international organisation’ – Constituent elements – Interpretation of the international agreement establishing the organisation – Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties – Articles 31 and 32 – Non-contractual liability)

In Case C‑790/24 P,

APPEAL under Article 56 of the Statute of the Court of Justice of the European Union, brought on 14 November 2024,

International Management Group (IMG), established in Brussels (Belgium), represented by J.‑Y. de Cara and L. Levi, avocats,

appellant,

the other party to the proceedings being:

European Commission, represented by J. Baquero Cruz, J.‑F. Brakeland and L. Puccio, acting as Agents,

defendant at first instance,

THE COURT (Fifth Chamber),

composed of M.L. Arastey Sahún, President of the Chamber, J. Passer, E. Regan, D. Gratsias (Rapporteur) and B. Smulders, Judges,

Advocate General: J. Richard de la Tour,

Registrar: F. Cathagne, Administrator,

having regard to the written procedure and further to the hearing on 11 December 2025,

after hearing the Opinion of the Advocate General at the sitting on 12 March 2026,

gives the following

Judgment

1 | By its appeal, International Management Group (IMG) seeks to have set aside the judgment of the General Court of the European Union of 4 September 2024, IMG v Commission (T‑509/21, the judgment under appeal, EU:T:2024:590), by which the General Court dismissed its action seeking, first, annulment of the decision of 8 June 2021 by which the European Commission refused to accord it, with retroactive effect from 16 December 2014, the status of an international organisation provided for by the EU Financial Regulations for the implementation of EU funds using the indirect management method (‘the decision at issue’) and, second, compensation for the material and non-material damage which it claims to have sustained. 
---|--- 
 
Legal context

International law

2 | Article 2(1) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties of 23 May 1969 (United Nations Treaty Series, Vol. 1155, p. 331; ‘the Vienna Convention’) provides: ‘For the purposes of the present Convention: | (a) | “treaty” means an international agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law, whether embodied in a single instrument or in two or more related instruments and whatever its particular designation; 
---|--- 
 
…

(i) | “international organisation” means an intergovernmental organisation.’ 
---|--- 
3 | Article 5 of that convention states that it ‘applies to any treaty which is the constituent instrument of an international organisation without prejudice to any relevant rules of the organisation’. 
---|--- 
4 | Under Article 31 of the Vienna Convention, entitled ‘General rule of interpretation’: ‘1. A treaty shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose. 2\. The context for the purpose of the interpretation of a treaty shall comprise, in addition to the text, including its preamble and annexes: | (a) | any agreement relating to the treaty which was made between all the parties in connection with the conclusion of the treaty; 
---|--- 
(b) | any instrument which was made by one or more parties in connection with the conclusion of the treaty and accepted by the other parties as an instrument related to the treaty. 
---|--- 
 
3\. There shall be taken into account, together with the context:

(a) | any subsequent agreement between the parties regarding the interpretation of the treaty or the application of its provisions; 
---|--- 
(b) | any subsequent practice in the application of the treaty which establishes the agreement of the parties regarding its interpretation; 
---|--- 
 
…

4\. A special meaning shall be given to a term if it is established that the parties so intended.’ 
 
5 | Article 32 of that convention, entitled ‘Supplementary means of interpretation’, is worded as follows: ‘Recourse may be had to supplementary means of interpretation, including the preparatory work of the treaty and the circumstances of its conclusion, in order to confirm the meaning resulting from the application of Article 31, or to determine the meaning when the interpretation according to Article 31: | (a) | leaves the meaning ambiguous or obscure; or 
---|--- 
(b) | leads to a result which is manifestly absurd or unreasonable.’ 
---|--- 
 
European Union law

The 2002 Financial Regulation

6 | Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1605/2002 of 25 June 2002 on the Financial Regulation applicable to the general budget of the European Communities (OJ 2002 L 248, p. 1), as amended by Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1995/2006 of 13 December 2006 (OJ 2006 L 390, p. 1) (‘the 2002 Financial Regulation’), was repealed with effect from 1 January 2013 by Regulation (EU, Euratom) No 966/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2012 on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union and repealing Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1605/2002 (OJ 2012 L 298, p. 1) (‘the 2012 Financial Regulation’). However, Article 212(a) of the 2012 Financial Regulation provided, inter alia, that Article 53 and Article 53d of the 2002 Financial Regulation were to continue to apply to all commitments made up to 31 December 2013. 
---|--- 
7 | Article 53 of the 2002 Financial Regulation provided: ‘The Commission shall implement the budget in accordance with the provisions set out in Articles 53a to 53d in any of the following ways: | (a) | on a centralised basis; 
---|--- 
(b) | by shared or decentralised management; 
---|--- 
(c) | by joint management with international organisations.’ 
---|--- 
8 | Article 53d of that regulation provided: ‘1. Where the Commission implements the budget by joint management, certain implementation tasks shall be delegated to international organisations … … 2\. Individual agreements concluded with international organisations for the award of financing shall contain detailed provisions for the implementation of the tasks entrusted to such international organisations. …’ 
---|--- 
 
The 2002 Financial Implementing Regulation

9 | Commission Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 2342/2002 of 23 December 2002 laying down detailed rules for the implementation of Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1605/2002 on the Financial Regulation applicable to the general budget of the European Communities (OJ 2002 L 357, p. 1), as amended by Commission Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 478/2007 of 23 April 2007 (OJ 2007 L 111, p. 13) (‘the 2002 Financial Implementing Regulation’), was repealed, with effect from 1 January 2013, by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 1268/2012 of 29 October 2012 on the rules of application of Regulation (EU, Euratom) No 966/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union (OJ 2012 L 362, p. 1) (‘the 2012 Delegated Financial Regulation’). 
---|--- 
10 | Article 43 of the 2002 Financial Implementing Regulation, entitled ‘Joint management’, provided, in paragraph 2 thereof: ‘The international organisations referred to in Article 53d of [the 2002 Financial] Regulation shall be: | (a) | international public-sector organisations set up by intergovernmental agreements, and specialised agencies set up by such organisations; 
---|--- 
 
…’ 
 
The 2012 Financial Regulation

11 | The 2012 Financial Regulation entered into force on 27 October 2012, in accordance with the first paragraph of Article 214 thereof. It was applicable from 1 January 2013 by virtue of the second paragraph of that article, without prejudice to the specific dates of application provided for in that paragraph for certain provisions of that regulation. 
---|--- 
12 | Among those provisions was Article 58 of that regulation, entitled ‘Methods of implementation of the budget’, which was applicable only to commitments made as from 1 January 2014. Paragraph 1 of that article was worded as follows: ‘The Commission shall implement the budget in the following ways: | (a) | directly (“direct management”), by its departments, …; 
---|--- 
(b) | under shared management with Member States (“shared management”); or 
---|--- 
(c) | indirectly (“indirect management”) … by entrusting budget implementation tasks to: 
---|--- 
 
…

(ii) | international organisations and their agencies; 
---|--- 
 
…’ 
 
The 2012 Delegated Financial Regulation

13 | Article 43 of the 2012 Delegated Financial Regulation, entitled ‘Specific provisions for indirect management with international organisations’, stated, in paragraph 1 thereof: ‘The international organisations referred to in point (ii) of Article 58(1)(c) of the [2012 Financial] Regulation shall be: | (a) | international public-sector organisations set up by intergovernmental agreements, and specialised agencies set up by such organisations; 
---|--- 
 
…’ 
 
Background to the dispute

14 | The background to the dispute, as set out in paragraphs 2 to 24 of the judgment under appeal, may, for the purposes of the present case, be summarised as follows. 
---|--- 
15 | The appellant, which was initially named International Management Group – Infrastructure for Bosnia and Herzegovina (IMG-IBH), was created on 25 November 1994 to provide the States and international organisations participating in the reconstruction of Bosnia and Herzegovina with an entity specifically created for that purpose. Since then, it has gradually extended its activities into the fields of reconstruction and development. 
---|--- 
16 | On 7 November 2013, the Commission adopted Implementing Decision C(2013) 7682 final on the Annual Action Programme 2013 in favour of Myanmar/Burma to be financed from the general budget of the European Union. That decision provided, inter alia, for a programme for trade development the cost of which, estimated at EUR 10 million, was to be financed by the European Union and implemented by joint management with the appellant. 
---|--- 
17 | On 17 February 2014, the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) informed the Commission that it had opened an investigation into the appellant’s status. On 15 December 2014, the Commission received the report drawn up by OLAF at the end of its investigation, in which OLAF considered, in essence, that the appellant was not an international organisation within the meaning of the 2002 Financial Regulation and the 2012 Financial Regulation. 
---|--- 
18 | On 16 December 2014, the Commission decided to entrust the implementation, using the indirect management method, of the trade development programme provided for in Implementing Decision C(2013) 7682 final, referred to in paragraph 16 of the present judgment, to an organisation other than the appellant (‘the decision of 16 December 2014’). 
---|--- 
19 | On 8 May 2015, the Commission sent a letter to the appellant informing it that it had decided, inter alia, that, until there was absolute certainty regarding the appellant’s status as an international organisation, it would not enter into any new delegation agreement with it using the indirect management method provided for by the 2012 Financial Regulation (‘the decision of 8 May 2015’). 
---|--- 
20 | By a first application lodged at the Registry of the General Court on 21 January 2015 and registered under case number T‑29/15, and then by a second application lodged at the same registry on 14 July 2015 and registered under case number T‑381/15, the appellant brought actions seeking, first, annulment of the decision of 16 December 2014 and, second, annulment of the decision of 8 May 2015 and for compensation for the damage caused to it by that decision. Those actions were dismissed by the judgments of 2 February 2017, International Management Group v Commission (T‑29/15, EU:T:2017:56), and of 2 February 2017, IMG v Commission (T‑381/15, EU:T:2017:57). By two appeals lodged on 11 April 2017 and registered, respectively, under case numbers C‑183/17 P and C‑184/17 P, the appellant sought to have those two judgments set aside. 
---|--- 
21 | By judgment of 31 January 2019, International Management Group v Commission (C‑183/17 P and C‑184/17 P, ‘the judgment of 31 January 2019’, EU:C:2019:78), the Court of Justice set aside the judgments of the General Court referred to in the preceding paragraph, itself ruled on the actions for annulment of the decisions of 16 December 2014 and 8 May 2015, annulled those decisions and referred Case T‑381/15 back to the General Court for it to rule on the action in that case, in so far as that action sought compensation for the damage allegedly sustained by the appellant as a result of the adoption of the decision of 8 May 2015. 
---|--- 
22 | By letter of 6 May 2019, the Commission requested that the appellant, in the context of compliance with the judgment of 31 January 2019, produce certain documents in order for it to demonstrate that it did in fact fulfil the requirements to be able to work with the Commission using the indirect management method. When the appellant did not produce the documents requested, the Commission, by letter of 18 July 2019, repeated its request for the production of documents, stating that, in the event of a refusal on the appellant’s part, it would turn directly to the States which the appellant considered to be its members. 
---|--- 
23 | On 26 November 2019, the Commission asked the States which the appellant considered to be its members whether they considered the appellant to be an international organisation, whether they were members of that organisation, and whether they had signed an international or intergovernmental agreement establishing the appellant as an international organisation. Should their answer be in the affirmative, they were requested to send the Commission a certified copy of that agreement and proof that its signatories had full powers to sign it, or a copy of the instrument of ratification of that agreement. The Commission repeated that request to some of those States on 27 January, 11 March, 25 May and 14 October 2020. 
---|--- 
24 | After informing the appellant, by letter of 19 February 2021, that it intended to adopt a decision refusing to accord it the status of an international organisation, the Commission invited it to submit observations, which the appellant did on 5 and 30 March 2021. 
---|--- 
25 | On 8 June 2021, the Commission adopted the decision at issue. 
---|--- 
 
The procedure before the General Court and the judgment under appeal

26 | By application lodged at the Registry of the General Court on 18 August 2021, the appellant brought an action seeking, in the first place, annulment of the decision at issue and, in the second place, an order that the Commission pay it, first, compensation in the amount of EUR 20000 for the damage which it claims to have sustained as a result of the unreasonable length of time involved in the procedure for the adoption of the decision at issue and, second, compensation in the amount of EUR 23651903 for the financial and non-material damage which it claims to have sustained as a result of the unlawful acts vitiating the decision at issue, which replaced the decisions of 16 December 2014 and 8 May 2015. 
---|--- 
27 | As a preliminary point, the General Court ruled, inter alia, on the admissibility of Annexes A.24 to the application and C.1 to the reply, which it declared inadmissible. 
---|--- 
28 | More specifically, as regards Annex A.24 to the application, the admissibility of which had been disputed by the Commission, the General Court found, in paragraphs 45 and 46 of the judgment under appeal, that that annex consisted of an opinion of the Commission’s Legal Service, the disclosure of which had not been authorised by that institution and which did not relate to a legislative procedure in respect of which greater openness was required. The General Court added that the appellant had not indicated any interest other than that of being able to rely on that legal opinion in the context of the dispute, and therefore its production did not appear to be guided by an overriding public interest. 
---|--- 
29 | It is apparent from paragraphs 58, 59, 92 and 190 of the judgment under appeal that, before the General Court, the appellant had put forward four pleas in law in support of its claim for annulment. According to the General Court, the first plea was divided into three parts, alleging, first, infringement of Article 266 TFEU and of the force of res judicata attaching to the judgment of 31 January 2019, second, infringement of the EU Financial Regulations and the Commission Guidelines of 7 January 2015 on the assessment of the status of international organisations and the possibility to assimilate non-profit organisations to international organisations, several errors of law, and breaches of various principles including, in particular, the principle of non-retroactivity and, third, breach of the principle of equal treatment. The second plea was also divided into three parts, alleging infringement of the obligation to state reasons, breach of the duty of diligence and breach of the obligation of impartiality. The third plea alleged breach of the principle of legal certainty. Last, the fourth plea was divided into three parts, alleging manifest errors of assessment and errors in law resulting from, in respect of the first part, the fact that the Commission did not correctly identify the appellant’s members, in respect of the second part, the fact that it refused to classify the act establishing the appellant as an international agreement establishing an international organisation and, in respect of the third part, the fact that it refused to recognise the appellant’s status as an international organisation notwithstanding the subsequent practice of its members and the recognition of that status by the European Union and some third countries. 
---|--- 
30 | The General Court examined, first, the first part of the second plea, then the first to fourth pleas and, last, the second and third parts of the second plea. It considered that those pleas, like the appellant’s claim for annulment, had to be rejected. 
---|--- 
31 | In particular, the fourth plea was examined in paragraphs 190 to 370 of the judgment under appeal. In that regard, the General Court, in the first place, set out, in paragraphs 190 to 213 of the judgment under appeal, certain preliminary considerations concerning the definition of the concept of ‘international organisation’ provided for by the EU Financial Regulations. It follows, in essence, that the General Court considered that the concepts of ‘international organisation’ and ‘international agreement’ referred to in the EU Financial Regulations had to be interpreted in the light of the relevant rules of international law, while being interpreted narrowly, in order to protect the financial interests of the European Union. 
---|--- 
32 | In the second place, in paragraphs 215 to 232 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined the first complaint in the first part of the fourth plea, alleging that the Commission made a manifest error of assessment in that it drew an artificial distinction between the appellant’s founding States, the contributing States and the States participating in the appellant’s bodies, namely the steering committee and the Government Support Group (‘GSG’). In that regard, in paragraphs 216 and 217 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court noted that it was not apparent from the statement of reasons for the decision at issue that the Commission had formally drawn such a distinction. 
---|--- 
33 | Nevertheless, in paragraphs 218 to 231 of that judgment, the General Court examined the scenario in which the decision at issue could be interpreted as drawing a distinction such as that alleged by the appellant. Following an analysis of the wording of the document of 25 November 1994 concerning the establishment of IMG-IBH (‘the resolution of 25 November 1994’), and of the appellant’s statute, the General Court found, in paragraph 230 of that judgment, that only those States and international organisations which had applied for admission to the appellant’s steering committee or standing committee, whose application had not given rise to objections from the members of that decision-making body, and which continued to sit on the committee on 16 December 2014 and, where appropriate, beyond that date, were to be regarded as being members of the appellant on the date on which the decision at issue took effect. On the basis of that finding, the General Court held, in paragraphs 231 and 232 of the judgment under appeal, that the appellant was not justified in criticising the Commission for not having considered certain States and certain international organisations to be its members if those States or organisations had not sat on its steering committee or standing committee since 16 December 2014 and that, therefore, the first complaint in the first part of the fourth plea had to be dismissed as unfounded. 
---|--- 
34 | In the third place, in paragraphs 233 to 248 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined the second complaint in the first part of the fourth plea, alleging a manifest error of assessment on the part of the Commission, vitiating the interpretation of the positions adopted by the Belgian and Austrian authorities. 
---|--- 
35 | First, as regards the Austrian authorities’ reply, it is apparent from paragraphs 235 to 239 of the judgment under appeal that the General Court found, in essence, that the Commission had not committed a manifest error of assessment in respect of that reply, since it had faithfully reproduced it in the decision at issue, while taking the view that it did not call into question the conclusion reached in that decision. 
---|--- 
36 | Second, as regards the Belgian authorities’ reply, it is apparent from paragraphs 241 and 242 of the judgment under appeal that the General Court considered that the Commission faithfully reproduced, in the decision at issue, the content of that reply. In addition, the General Court rejected the appellant’s argument that the Kingdom of Belgium had to be regarded as one of its members. Therefore, in paragraph 248 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court dismissed the second complaint in the first part of the fourth plea. 
---|--- 
37 | In the fourth place, in paragraphs 249 to 257 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined the third complaint in the first part of the fourth plea, alleging errors of law and a manifest error of assessment on the part of the Commission in refusing to recognise that the European Union had become a member of the appellant. The General Court rejected that complaint, first, on the ground, as is apparent from paragraphs 253 and 254 of the judgment under appeal, that the Commission had no longer sat on the appellant’s steering committee with effect from 20 May 2003 and that, consequently, the European Union could not be regarded as a member of the appellant during the effective period of the decision at issue. Second, in paragraph 255 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court found that the appellant had neither established nor even claimed that, on the date on which the decision at issue took effect, its members included another international organisation. Since all the complaints put forward in support of the first part of the appellant’s fourth plea had been dismissed, the General Court considered that that part had to be dismissed in its entirety. 
---|--- 
38 | In the fifth place, in paragraphs 260 to 303 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined the first complaint in the second part of the fourth plea, alleging errors of law in that the Commission refused to classify the resolution of 25 November 1994 as an international agreement. 
---|--- 
39 | In that regard, the General Court found, in paragraphs 273 and 274 of the judgment under appeal, that that resolution did contain at least one legally binding commitment for its signatories and that the Commission had vitiated the decision at issue by an error of law in adopting the position of the Republic of Austria and the Republic of Finland, according to which that resolution constituted a political declaration which was not legally binding. 
---|--- 
40 | In addition, in paragraph 289 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court held that the Commission had vitiated the decision at issue by an error of law in refusing to classify the resolution of 25 November 1994 as an international agreement on account of the absence of full powers of the participants in the meeting of the same day at which that resolution was adopted, since the signature of that resolution was subsequently confirmed by at least two States. 
---|--- 
41 | Furthermore, in paragraphs 295 and 299 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court found, in essence, that the Commission had not erred in law in asking the appellant’s Member States to specify whether they had signed the resolution of 25 November 1994 and, if necessary, to produce any instruments of signature or ratification of that resolution. 
---|--- 
42 | At the end of its examination of the first complaint in the second part of the fourth plea, the General Court held, in essence, in paragraphs 302 and 303 of the judgment under appeal, that the Commission’s errors of law referred to in paragraphs 39 and 40 of the present judgment were not, by themselves, such as to entail the annulment of the decision at issue. According to the General Court, it would still be necessary to determine whether the appellant had been founded by an international agreement the purpose of which was to establish it as an international organisation. 
---|--- 
43 | In the sixth place, in paragraphs 304 to 319 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined the second complaint in the second part of the fourth plea, alleging an error of interpretation as to the intention of the signatories to the resolution of 25 November 1994 to grant the appellant the status of an international organisation. Following an analysis of the wording, purpose and context of that resolution, the General Court concluded, in paragraph 319 of that judgment, that the Commission had not erred in finding that that resolution had neither the object nor the effect of conferring on the appellant the status of an international organisation. Accordingly, the General Court held that the second complaint in the second part of the appellant’s fourth plea had to be rejected as unfounded, as did, consequently, that part in its entirety. 
---|--- 
44 | In the seventh place, in paragraphs 321 to 347 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined the first complaint in the third part of the appellant’s fourth plea, alleging an error of law as regards the subsequent practice of the signatories to the resolution of 25 November 1994 demonstrating a sufficiently wide and clear recognition of the appellant’s status as an international organisation. 
---|--- 
45 | In that regard, the General Court held, in paragraph 329 of the judgment under appeal, that, in accordance with the judgment of the International Court of Justice of 31 March 2014, Whaling in the Antarctic (Australia v. Japan; New Zealand intervening), I.C.J. Reports 2014, p. 226), demonstrating that subsequent agreements or a subsequent practice of the signatories to the resolution of 25 November 1994 have altered the interpretation of the provisions of that resolution in order to confer on the appellant the status of an international organisation was subject to the condition that all the signatories to that resolution or, at least, all of the appellant’s members had approved such an amendment. 
---|--- 
46 | The General Court found, in paragraph 330 of the judgment under appeal, first, that the appellant’s statute adopted on 10 March 1995 (‘the initial statute’) conferred legal personality on it and provided that some of its staff would benefit from immunities and, second, that Article 1 of the appellant’s statute adopted in 2012 (‘the 2012 statute’) classified it as an international organisation. Nevertheless, in paragraph 331 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court found that the appellant had not established that those two statutes reflected the intention of all the signatories to the resolution of 25 November 1994 or, at least, of its members, to confer on it the status of an international organisation. The General Court set out the grounds for that finding in paragraphs 332 to 345 of the judgment under appeal. It therefore concluded, in paragraphs 346 and 347 of that judgment, that the Commission had not erred in law in finding that the practice subsequent to the adoption of the resolution of 25 November 1994, and then to the adoption of the appellant’s initial statute and 2012 statute, did not demonstrate a sufficiently wide and clear recognition of the appellant’s status as an international organisation and that, consequently, the first complaint in the third part of the fourth plea had to be dismissed as unfounded. 
---|--- 
47 | In the eighth place, in paragraphs 348 to 365 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined and rejected the second complaint in the third part of the appellant’s fourth plea, alleging errors of law in that the Commission failed to take account of the recognition of the appellant’s status as an international organisation by the European Union and certain States. 
---|--- 
48 | In that regard, the General Court, first, in paragraphs 349 to 359 of the judgment under appeal, examined and rejected the appellant’s argument that the conclusion of agreements between itself and the Commission under joint or indirect management necessarily entailed an obligation on the part of that institution to recognise its status as an international organisation. 
---|--- 
49 | Second, in paragraphs 360 to 365 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined and rejected the appellant’s argument alleging an error of law in that the Commission did not take into account the headquarters agreements concluded by the appellant. As is apparent from paragraph 364 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court considered that the fact that States which have not acceded to the agreement forming an organisation and which are not, or are no longer, members of it consider it to be an international organisation does not entail any obligation on the Commission to recognise that organisation as having the status of an international organisation. 
---|--- 
50 | In the ninth place, in paragraphs 366 to 370 of the judgment under appeal, the General Court examined and rejected the third complaint in the third part of the appellant’s fourth plea, alleging an error of law in that the Commission had failed to take account of the fact that the appellant’s members had not dissolved it and the fact that it complied with the principle of speciality. The General Court acknowledged, in paragraph 367 of that judgment, that the signatories to the resolution of 25 November 1994 which became members of the appellant intended, when the appellant’s 2008 statute and 2012 statute were adopted, to provide it with a degree of stability and to entrust it with specialised tasks in the field of reconstruction and development beyond the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It nevertheless held, in paragraphs 368 and 369 of that judgment, that, in so far as neither the signatories to the resolution of 25 November 1994 nor the appellant’s members had demonstrated an intention unanimously or, at least by majority, to confer on it the status of an international organisation, the fact that the appellant had not been dissolved had no bearing on the lawfulness of the decision at issue. The General Court therefore dismissed the third complaint in the third part of the fourth plea and, consequently, that part and that plea in their entirety. 
---|--- 
51 | The appellant’s claim for compensation was examined in paragraphs 418 to 447 of the judgment under appeal. In that regard, the General Court found, in paragraph 418 of that judgment, that the appellant put forward two heads of damage in respect of which it claimed, respectively, compensation in the amount of EUR 20000 on account of the allegedly unreasonable length of time involved in the procedure for the adoption of the decision at issue and compensation in the amount of EUR 23651903 for the financial and non-material damage which it attributed to the unlawful acts vitiating the decision at issue, which had replaced the decisions of 16 December 2014 and 8 May 2015. 
---|--- 
52 | The first head of damage, which was examined in paragraphs 429 to 442 of the judgment under appeal, was rejected on the grounds, as set out in paragraphs 440 to 442 of that judgment, that the time taken by the Commission to prepare and adopt the decision at issue was not unreasonable and that the appellant had not established the existence of material or non-material damage resulting from the infringement alleged. 
---|--- 
53 | The second head of damage, which was examined in paragraphs 443 to 447 of the judgment under appeal, was rejected on the grounds, as set out in paragraphs 444 and 446 of that judgment, that the claims seeking annulment of the decision at issue had been dismissed, and therefore the condition for the European Union to incur non-contractual liability, relating to the existence of a breach of a rule of law intended to confer rights on individuals, had not been satisfied and that, moreover, the appellant had not relied, in support of that second head of damage, on heads of unlawfulness which differed from those which it set out in support of its claims for annulment. 
---|--- 
54 | Consequently, the General Court dismissed the appellant’s action in its entirety. 
---|--- 
 
Forms of order sought

55 | The appellant claims that the Court should set aside the judgment under appeal, rule itself on its action, uphold that action and order the Commission to pay the costs of both the proceedings before the General Court and those before the Court of Justice. 
---|--- 
56 | The Commission contends that the Court should dismiss the appeal and order the appellant to pay the costs. 
---|--- 
 
The appeal

57 | The appellant relies on seven grounds in support of its appeal. The first ground of appeal alleges infringement of Article 266 TFEU and of the General Court’s obligation to state reasons for its judgments, breach of the prohibition on ruling ultra petita and of the principle of non-retroactivity and distortion of the evidence in the file. The second ground of appeal alleges breach of the principle of res judicata and of the obligation to state reasons. The third ground of appeal alleges breach of the principle of equal treatment and of the rights of the defence. The fourth ground of appeal alleges breach of the principle of legal certainty and of the obligation to state reasons. The fifth ground of appeal alleges an error of law in that the General Court rejected the fourth plea in the appellant’s action. The sixth ground of appeal alleges breach of the principle of good administration and of the duty of diligence, and infringement of Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. Last, the seventh ground of appeal alleges breach of the principle audi alteram partem and of the principle of equality of arms. 
---|--- 
 
The seventh ground of appeal

Arguments of the parties

58 | By the seventh ground of appeal, which it is appropriate to examine first, the appellant challenges the grounds that were set out in paragraphs 38 to 47 of the judgment under appeal to justify the General Court’s decision to declare Annex A.24 to the application lodged before the General Court inadmissible. 
---|--- 
59 | In the first place, the appellant claims that it was the General Court itself which, at the hearing before it, took the initiative to ask the Commission whether it objected to that annex being retained in the case file. In so doing, the General Court altered the subject matter of the dispute and ruled ultra petita. 
---|--- 
60 | In the second place, the appellant submits that the circumstances of the present case are different from those of the case which gave rise to the judgment of 16 February 2022, Hungary v Parliament and Council (C‑156/21, EU:C:2022:97, paragraphs 54 to 56), on which the General Court relied. The appellant submits that the opinion of the Commission’s Legal Service in Annex A.24 to the application before the General Court is in the public domain following a leak in the press. It follows, according to the appellant, that that opinion, having regard to its nature and the conditions of its disclosure, did not undermine either confidentiality or an overriding public interest. Moreover, that opinion is a decisive document, relating exclusively to the case before the General Court. 
---|--- 
61 | In the third place, the appellant relies on ‘the principle of equality of arms in a fair trial’, which means, in its view, that each party must be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present its case, including evidence, under conditions that do not place it at a ‘substantial disadvantage’ vis-à-vis its opponent. The appellant therefore claims that the General Court should have retained Annex A.24 to the application in the case file and erred in law in declaring it inadmissible. 
---|--- 
62 | The Commission contends that the seventh ground of appeal must be rejected. 
---|--- 
 
Findings of the Court

63 | In the first place, as regards the appellant’s argument that the General Court ruled ultra petita in deciding to remove Annex A.24 to the application from the file, it is apparent from paragraph 38 of the judgment under appeal that, at the hearing before the General Court, the Commission had raised the inadmissibility of that annex, in that it included an opinion of its Legal Service. 
---|--- 
64 | It follows that the General Court decided to remove that annex from the case file at the request of the Commission and, accordingly, it cannot, in any event, be criticised for ruling ultra petita. It is irrelevant, in that regard, that the Commission raised the inadmissibility of that annex in response to a question from the General Court. 
---|---

The action

161 | In accordance with the first paragraph of Article 61 of the Statute of the Court of Justice of the European Union, where the state of the whole or a part of the proceedings so permits, the Court of Justice may itself give final judgment on the whole of the proceedings, or, as the case may be, on the part thereof the state of which so permits, while referring, where appropriate, the part the state of which does not so permit back to the General Court. 
---|--- 
162 | In the present case, the Court of Justice will itself give final judgment on the claim for annulment of the decision at issue and on part of the claim for compensation. 
---|--- 
 
The claim for annulment

163 | By the second and fourth pleas in its action, the appellant complains that the Commission, in essence, vitiated the decision at issue by errors of law and manifest errors of assessment which led it to find that the appellant was not an international organisation and, therefore, was not eligible for the implementation of the EU budget under the indirect management method provided for by the EU Financial Regulations. 
---|--- 
164 | It must be borne in mind that the General Court held that the Commission had erred in law in finding, in the decision at issue, that the resolution of 25 November 1994 did not constitute an international agreement. There is no need to call that finding into question, since the Commission did not lodge a cross-appeal challenging that part of the judgment under appeal (see, to that effect, judgment of 23 November 2021, Council v Hamas, C‑833/19 P, EU:C:2021:950, paragraph 81 and the case-law cited). 
---|--- 
165 | As is apparent from paragraphs 136 and 138 of the present judgment, the wording and purpose of the resolution of 25 November 1994 do not support the finding that the authors of that resolution did not intend to establish the appellant as an international organisation, or that their intention was to establish the appellant as a mere mechanism for cooperation between them, without independent legal personality. 
---|--- 
166 | On the contrary, it is apparent from that resolution that those authors endowed the appellant with its own bodies, namely the General Manager, appointed by that resolution, and the steering committee and the GSG, with its own staff and its own budget. In addition, powers such as those referred to in paragraph 134 of the present judgment were conferred on the appellant. All of those factors show that the authors of that resolution intended the appellant to constitute a separate entity, enjoying a degree of autonomy vis-à-vis its members, which, moreover, were liable to vary, in so far as it was, in essence, provided for that each member of the appellant could, at any time, unilaterally decide to terminate its participation in the appellant. 
---|--- 
167 | In so far as those authors intended to establish the appellant as a separate entity, enjoying a degree of autonomy, it follows that those authors also intended to confer on the appellant international legal personality, since those factors entail the appellant’s capacity to exercise rights and be subject to obligations of its own in the international legal order and the capacity to act. 
---|--- 
168 | That finding is not called into question by the replies given by the States referred to on the appellant’s website – and presented there as its members – to the questions sent to them by the Commission concerning the adoption of the resolution of 25 November 1994 and the appellant’s status. 
---|--- 
169 | It must be observed in that regard that those replies are opinions that were given 25 years after the adoption of the resolution of 25 November 1994. As the Advocate General observed, in essence, in points 218 and 219 of his Opinion, such opinions are not relevant for the purpose of assessing the intention of the parties when signing the resolution of 25 November 1994. 
---|--- 
170 | As regards the fact that all the States questioned by the Commission, with the exception of the Republic of Austria, had stated that they were not members of the appellant, it should be noted that the question of whether a State is a member of an entity is distinct from the question of whether that entity constitutes an international organisation. It cannot be ruled out that certain States or international organisations which participated in the creation of the appellant through the resolution of 25 November 1994 and which, as a result, became members of the appellant, subsequently left the appellant and were no longer members of it, without that affecting the appellant’s status as an international organisation. 
---|--- 
171 | In any event, once established, an international organisation does not simply cease to exist if some of its members decide to leave it. As the case may be, it is for the remaining members to decide whether or not to dissolve the organisation concerned, while at the same time taking the necessary steps to settle the legal relationships entered into by that organisation during its existence. It is not apparent from the decision at issue that, during the approximately 27 years that have passed since the resolution of 25 November 1994 was adopted, the decision was taken to dissolve the appellant. 
---|--- 
172 | On the basis of all the foregoing considerations, it must be held that the decision at issue is vitiated by illegality, in so far as the Commission found, in breach of Article 43(1) of the 2012 Delegated Financial Regulation and Article 31 of the Vienna Convention, which reflects customary international law, that the resolution of 25 November 1994 did not constitute an international agreement that had the effect of establishing the appellant as an international organisation. Accordingly, the decision at issue must be annulled.

The claim for compensation

173 | The appellant claims that the Commission should be ordered to pay it compensation in the amount of EUR 8651903 for the material damage and in the amount of EUR 15 million for the non-material damage which it claims to have sustained as a result of the unlawful acts vitiating the decision at issue, which replaced the decisions of 16 December 2014 and 8 May 2015. 
---|--- 
174 | In the first place, as regards the claim for compensation for the non-material damage, the appellant recalls that, in a previous case before the General Court, it had sought compensation in the amount of EUR 10 million for the non-material damage which it claimed to have sustained as a result of the adoption of the decision of 8 May 2015. It claims that that non-material damage ‘has increased by EUR 5 million’ as a result of the adoption of the decision at issue. 
---|--- 
175 | It should be noted in that regard that, by the judgment of 22 September 2022, IMG v Commission (C‑619/20 P and C‑620/20 P, EU:C:2022:722), the Court of Justice set aside the judgment of 9 September 2020, IMG v Commission (T‑381/15 RENV, EU:T:2020:406), in so far as the General Court had rejected as unfounded, inter alia, an earlier claim for compensation made by the appellant for the non-material damage which it claimed to have sustained as a result of the adoption of the decision of 8 May 2015. 
---|--- 
176 | Ruling, after disposing of the case, on the substance of that claim, the Court of Justice noted that the sufficiently serious breach by the Commission, when it adopted the decision of 8 May 2015, of its duty of diligence had indeed been established and that that breach had caused the appellant non-material damage in the form of damage to its reputation. However, the Court recalled that it had found that that decision was unlawful and had annulled it by the judgment of 31 January 2019. The Court therefore held that the clear terms in which the finding that that decision was unlawful was worded were such as to ensure appropriate and sufficient compensation for the non-material damage sustained by the appellant, having regard to the context in which they were made, and, accordingly, the appellant’s claim for damages had to be dismissed as unfounded in so far as it related to the non-material damage resulting from the unlawfulness of the decision of 8 May 2015 (judgment of 22 September 2022, IMG v Commission, C‑619/20 P and C‑620/20 P, EU:C:2022:722, paragraphs 194 and 198 to 200). 
---|--- 
177 | The Court thus applied settled case-law, according to which non-material damage or non-pecuniary damage may, in certain situations, be regarded as being remedied appropriately and sufficiently by the annulment of the unlawful act which caused it (judgment of 22 September 2022, IMG v Commission, C‑619/20 P and C‑620/20 P, EU:C:2022:722, paragraph 197 and the case-law cited). 
---|--- 
178 | In accordance with that case-law and for reasons similar to those given by the Court with regard to the non-material damage sustained by the appellant as a result of the adoption of the decision of 8 May 2015, it must be held that the finding, in paragraph 172 of the present judgment, that the decision at issue is unlawful, expressed in clear terms, and the annulment of the decision at issue that flows from that finding are such as to ensure appropriate and sufficient compensation for the non-material damage sustained by the appellant as a result of the adoption of that decision. 
---|--- 
179 | In those circumstances, the claim for compensation must be rejected as unfounded, in so far as it seeks compensation for that non-material damage. 
---|--- 
180 | In the second place, as regards the claim for compensation for the material damage which the appellant claims to have sustained as a result of the unlawful acts vitiating the decision at issue, it should be noted that, admittedly, the concept of ‘international organisation’ may give rise to difficulties of interpretation in the absence, in particular, of case-law on that subject (judgment of 22 September 2022, IMG v Commission, C‑619/20 P and C‑620/20 P, EU:C:2022:722, paragraph 191).
